ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
*461. [The questioner (Shri Bratin Sen Gupta) was absent. For answer, 
vide page 22 infra.] 
Visit by Australian Foreign Minister to India 
*462. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the 
Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is fact that the Australian Foreign Minister visited India 
recently; 
(b) if so, what is the outcome of his visit; and 
(c) whether he indicated restoration of normalcy after the Pokhran Test 
in 1998? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT 
SINGH): (a) Yes, Sir. The Australian Foreign Minister Mr. Alexander Downer 
visited India from 21—24 March, 2000.  
(b) Mr. Downer called on the President and PM and separately met me  
and the Minister of Commerce and Industry. A range of bilateral and 
multilateral issues were discussed. Both countries agreed, in principle, to 
resume defence  relations. Mr. Downer exte nded me an invitation to visit 
Australia, which I have  accepted: With Shri Murasoli Maran Mr. Downer 
discussed issues relevant to Commerce and Industry. 
(c) Yes, Sir. Both sides agreed, in principle, to resume the defence 
relations which were broken off after the Pokhran tests in 1998. Modalities for 
this will be worked out.

SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Between May 1998 and the Australian 
Foreign Minister's visit the routine of visits between the two countries got 
interrupted. This was the first visit. This was -the hon. Member is right —
preceded by Mr. Tinfisher's visit who, as the hon. Members know, knows India 
very well and who is a former soldier. T hey have great regard for India. But he 
had really visited India as part of the commercial dialogue with our country. 
Neither with him nor with my distinguished counterpart, Mr. Alexander 
Downer, did the question of sports come up because I believe there i s sufficient 
sporting activity between India and Australia, whether it is in the field of tennis 
or cricket. In fact, perhaps there is an overdose of some of it. So, sports was not 
discussed. On the question of cities that you mentioned, development of tra de 
with those cities proper, the Indians currently living in Australia wishing to 
promote trade etc., yes, these were all discussed, and were discussed in much 
greater detail, when our Commerce Minister, Shri Murasoli Maran, a month 
after Mr. Alexander Dow ner's visit, went to Australia and held further detailed 
talks in regard to expanding commerce and trade ties. 
SHRI C.P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU: When Mr. Alexander Downer 
visited India, you had a dialogue with him. I would like to know whether any 
discussions where held with regard to CTBT and whether you agreed or refused 
to sign the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty. My next question is, on 12th April, 
Shri Murasolli Maran visited Australia and had discussions with the Trade 
Marks Minister there. As a result of the  discussion, I would like to know 
whether the sanctions imposed by the Australian Government will be revoked 
or not? 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: There are again two parts of the query . With 
your permission, Sir, I will take the second part first which relates to the visit by 
thy hon. Commerce Minister to Australia. Now, strictly, it is a question that he 
sould reply, but because the hon. Memebrs has taken the trouble to ask me, I 
might just throw a little light on the subject. So far as the trade sanctions are 
concerned, Australia did, certainly, in post -May 1998, announce the imposition 
of sanctions against India. But even after announcing the sanctions, like USA 
had done, Australia did not restrict any of its trading activity with India. It, in 
fact, continued to  encourrage; not simply the continuance of trade, but 
encouraged it to expand, as far as possible. As to whether, during Shri Murasoli 
Maran's visit the question of sanctions were duscussed between Shri Murasoli 
Maran and his counterpart it, it really a matter of detail which you should ask -
from him, and I am sure he will benefit you with the reply. On the second 
aspect, Sir, with your permission, if I might answer, it really relates to whether 
the

question of Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty and subscription to that treaty was 
taken up between Alexander Downer and myself. Australia, as know, since 
May 1998, has taken a certain postion on non- proliferation issue. This is a 
position which is a traditional position. We can hold a different view; and, 
indeed, we do hold a different view. We expressed a different view. I explained 
to Mr. Downer that India's position remains as it was announced by both the 
Prime Minister and myself at the UN General Assembly, and as repeated by the 
Prime Minister on a number of occasions in Parliament. Australia, earlier, had 
taken a rigid stand, which was a stand marked by some prescriptive message to 
India and demands on India. It is all now a thing of the past. Austrlia continues 
to hold a certain v iewpoint in regard to non- proliferation. India continues to 
hold a different viewpoint: and it is our endeavour to explain to each other the 
viewpoints that we hold, which are born of national consideration  and attempts 
to bring the distance between the two points as close as possible.

SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO: The main interest of the Australian, like 
that of many other countries, is the enormous consumer market that India 
provide. As far as India and Australia are concerned, the balance of trade is 
adverse, roughly in the ratio of 5; 1 in favour of Australia. The interest of the 
Australians, like that of the US and New and Zealand, is in vegetables and 
agricultural produce. I would like to know the steps that the Government has 
taken to see to it that farmers are, th erefore, not affected and our agricultural 
self-sufficiency is protected from this onslaught. 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: With your permission, Sir, let me disabuse the 
mind of the hon. Member: there is no onslaught from Australia. The hon. 
Member is correct that there is a great mismatch in the trading figures between 
India and Australia and mis mismatch is in Australia's favour. This mismatch is 
born, argely, on account of the strength that the Austrelian minerals have 
because we are importing them; it is largely a mismatch born of our dependence 
on certain kinds of Australian minerals. • 
The fact of the matter is, Australian exports to India is roughly 1.5 billion 
dollars and Indian exports to Australia is only 500 million dollars. So, the ratio 
is not as what is suggested —  5:11 am not scoring over you, but I just wanted to 
make this small point. The ratio between 1:5 billion and half -a-billion by itself 
is significant enough. Even though it might not be 1:5 the fact remains that 
Australia has certain strength in minerals. 
So far as agriculture is concerned, like vegetables and greens, as cited, I 
can assure the hon. Member that the tariff barriers against such imports are so 
structured by the Government that there is no way that any import of Australian 
foodgrains or fruits or other materials can take place at the cost of Indian 
producers or to the detriment of Indian agriculture.

*464. SHRI K.M KHAN: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) 
has carried out some research for preservation for foodgrains and vegetables; 
(b) if so, what extent this technology is being used in the country; 
(c) whether use of such technology for preservation of foodgrains and 
vegetables is safe and good for human life; and 
(d) if so, what specific proof Government have and what are the details 
thereof? 
THE MINISTER Of STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF ATOMIC 
ENERGY (SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid 
on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. The Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) has carried 
out extensive research for preser vation of meat & meat products, spices, 
foodgrains, viz, rice, wheat & wheat products, semolina (sooji, rawa) and 
vegetables viz. potatoes, onions, garlic, ginger, mushrooms etc. 
(b) After considerable R&D in this field, a small Pilot Scale Package 
Irradiator which can treat up to 500 kg of onion and potato per hour is being 
operated at Food Technology Division, Bhaba Atomic Research Centre, 
Mumbai. A facility for technology demonstration purpose has been 
commissioned by the Department of Atomic Energy for irradition of spices at 
Vashi, Navi Mumbai. Another demonstration facility for irradiation of 
potatoes, onions and other food products with need low dose irradiation is 
being set up at Lasalgaon in Nasik District of Maharashtra. 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) The Ministry of Healt h and Family Welfare, Govt. of India, New 
Delhi has amended suitably the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules (1955) 
in 1994 and given clearance for radiation processing of food has also been 
accepted by the World Health Organisation, Food & Agriculture O rganisation, 
International Atomic Energy Agency and Codex Alimentarious Commission 
which is responsible for setting up global food standards. A number of 
countreis are already using the radiation process for a variety of foods. 
SHRI K.M. KHAN: Sir, this technology is a very important and useful 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [27 April, 2000] 
development in the preservation of food. I would like to ask the hon. Minister 
whether this technology can be made available throughout the country or it 
would be usedhonly in areas co nfined to atomic research centres. What are the 
difficulties faced by the Government in providing such vital facilities all over 
the country? 
SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE: Sir, food security, as the hon. 
Member said, is a primaru importance for the self -reliance of any country. I do 
agree with it. This is one of the latest methods which has been developed for 
preserving food, with the least change in sensory quality. It involves exposure 
of food to short -wave energy, which allows you to extend its itshelf life,  
anything to do with insect disinfestation, anything which is carried like food 
borne pathogens and parasaites, as also anything like microbial decontamination 
of spices. It is eco -friendly. It consumes less energy. It has an operational 
simplicity, and it is the latest technology. 
Now, there are certain safety features that are to be followed, under this, 
the irradiation plants requires to be authorised by the Atomic Energy 
Regulatory Board. After this, the licence has to be obtained from the authority 
concerned — in this case, it is the Atomic energy Department — and it is to be 
issued only after ascertaining all the safety aspects of the installation and its 
suitability to ensure proper process controls, availability of licensed operations 
and qualified s taff. In some progressive States, the Food and Drug 
Administration also does this job. This is available, at the moment, in three 
Statas —  Goa, Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh. We have a small pilot project, 
which is food package irradiator, at the Food Tec hnology Division of BARC, 
in Mumbai, which can treat about five hundred kg. of onion and potato. 
There is one more which is under construction at Laselgaon as Nasik in 
Maharashtra. As far at this is cboncerned, we would be happy that these come 
up in other parts of the country provided the safety standards are taken care of, 
met and stringent quality is maintained. 
SHRI K.M. KHAN: Sir, my second supplementary is that this issue 
relates to the safety aspects. I would like to know whether the foodgrains and 
vegetables undergone through the atomic rays are indeed safe for human 
consumption and no side effects are there by using such preserved foodstuffs. 
SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE: Sir, the process itself involves 
passing the food through a radiation field which allows food sto absorb the 
desired radiatron energy and the studies that have been done show that this has 
very little effect on the nutrients itself. Sir, extensive studies on food irradiation  
8 

[27 April, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
have been conducted worldwide and experts of the WHO, FAO, international 
atomic energy agencies and we have jointly reviewed all the data that has been 
obtained worldwide, including from India, in the last four decades. They have 
declared that irradiated food is safe for human consumpt ion. The American 
Council for Science and Health, the American Medical Association, the 
National Institution of State Department of Agriculture, the Council of 
Agricultural Science and Technology and the American Dietetic Association 
have all endorsed the safety of the irradiated food. Today 38 other countries, 
apart from us, have approved the use of radiation in certain food items. 
DR. BIPLAB DASGUPTA: Sir, I fell that on this issue, I would say that 
we will be entering an unknown territory. We have been g iven a complete and 
impressive list of organisations and insitutions which have certified that this 
food is safe. But the point is that this is only one side of the picture. It is quite 
possible that the scientists from Britain may take a different positio n. I will 
give you a concrete example of genetically modify food. Now, America is 
trying to push genetically modified food all over the world. In Britain there is a 
lot of resistance to it. In fact, they are saying it is a right of the consumer to 
know whe ther it is genetically modified food or not and every shop has to 
advertise in this regard. Similarly, about the food which is subjected to 
radiation, we are yet to know its impacts. As you know, about nuclear energy it 
was said at one stage that it did no t affect environmentally, and all that. But 
later it was found that it pollutes the atmosphere in different ways. What I am 
asking is this. Is the hon. Minister satisifed with whatever has been told to her 
by the American establishment or has she been able to consult much more 
wider groups of scientists and technicians to know that this type of food is not 
contaminted by this process? 
SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE: Sir, I am sure that the hon. 
Member's apprehension is something that probably is shared by a lot of people 
because this is a very new technology. As this is a new technology, at the 
moment, we are in the process of sensitising a lot of people about it. But, I can 
say that we will do our best and we will have a certain amount of interaction 
with all con cerned. What I have just now told you on the floor of the House 
means that there is a lot of interaction going on. As far as the Atomic 
Regulatory Board is concerned, it takes extreme and stringent steps to see that 
we keep it within the safety standards. We will do our best remain within those 
safety standards. 
DR. MANMOHAN SINGH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, in our country we have 
an Atomic Regulatory Authority. I would like to know from the hon. Minister  
9 

RAJYA SABHA [27 April, 2000] 
whether this matter of low irradiation has ever been referred to mis Atomic 
Regulatory Authority and whether they have certified with regard to its safety. 
The second question is that if the Minister is so sure that this is perfectly a safe 
technology, then why are we limitinjg its use only to a small pilot scale project? 
SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE: Sir, first, I will reply to the second 
part of the question. We have, very recently, after the testing which was 
conducted at the BARC, started two centres —one at Nasik and the other one at 
Navi Mumbai. These facilities are still coming up. They are expensive facilities. 
They have to go through some very stringent testing and that has taken a certain 
amount of time. Also, the food and drug authority itself, in the States, is at 
various stages  of progress. The three States that are very progressive are: 
Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra and Goa. The other States, as far as mis issue is 
concerned, are still formulating the laws and rules. A certain amount of time has 
taken place. As I said, this would be dealt with. 
With regard to the second part of the supplementary. I would submit that 
it has been referred to the AERB. The AERB has laid down a very stringent set 
of guidelines, and those guideliens are to be followed before the licence is 
issued by the Department of Atomic Energy.

*467. DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA: Will the Minister of LABOUR 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether recommendations of the Bachhawat Wage Board and 
Manisana Wage Board Reports were accepted by Government for 
implementation; 
(b) if so, date of submission of such report, recommendations accepted, 
date of issue of notification and implementation status of each 
recommendation in various States and Union Territories; and 
(c) the reasons for non -implementation of  such report in Assam and 
targeted action contemplated to ensure its early compliance? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (DR. SATYA NARAYAN JATTYA): 
(a) and (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the house.

Statement 
The report of th e Bachawat Wage Board was submitted to the 
Government on 30.5.1989. The recommendations regarding pay scales, 
dearness allowance, house rent allowance, city compensatory allowance etc. 
were accepted by Government vide notifications dated 31.8.89 and the ra tes 
of house rent allowance and city compensatory allowance were modified by 
notification dated 21.0990. The responsibility for implementation of 
recommendations lies with state Governments. As per information received 
from State Governments, out of 1715 n ewspaper establishments, 643 have 
fully implemented and 26 have partially implemented the recommendations. 
A statement showing position of implementation in various States/Union 
Territories is enclosed at Statement-I. (See below) 
As regards recommendations  of Manisana Wage Board, the final 
recommendations have not been submitted to the Government. In October, 
1995, the Manisana Wage Board submitted Interim Report recommending 15 
% of the basic wage as interim relief to all newspapers employees. The 
Government notified the interim relief vide Notifications dated 24.9.96 
giving interim relief at the rate of 20% of the basic wage and an additional 
amount of Rs. 100/- p.m. w.e.f 204.1995. 
The Manisana Wage Board submitted tentative proposals to the 
Government on 21.12.1999 which were published in the Gazette on 
30.12.1999. The employers' and employees' organisations and other persons 
interested in the revision of rates of wages were required to submit their 
comments with respect to tentative proposals., In respon se to the above 
notice, 72 parties submitted their comments and 42 requested for oral 
hearings. The oral hearings on comments/objections were completed in three 
rounds during February 22-25, March 14-17 and March 27-31,2000. 
The meetings of the Manisana Wage Board to finalise the report were 
held during 17th to 20b April, 2000. The Board is yet to submit final report. 
As per information received from the Government of Assam, the 
Bachawat Wage Board Award has been implemented by four newspaper 
estalishments namely, Assam Tribune, Dainik Asom, Janambhumi and the 
Sentinel Group of Papers, out of a total of 74 newspaper establishments. 
It has further been reported that in a tripartite meeting held on 
30.10.1999 between representatives of newspaper employees, employers and 
government officials, a decision was taken to ask newspaper establishments 
to determine

Remumeration of Contract Employees in PSUs 
*463. SHRI DIPLIP SINGH JUDEV: Will the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that some public sector 
undertakings are appointing techni cal and non- technical persons as coatract 
employees on meagre remuneration; 
(b) if so, under what rules these employees are being engaged; 
(c) whether the service conditions of these employees are pitiable as  
compared to regular employees; and 
(d) if so, what step s Government propose to take to direct the various  
public sector undertakings for regularisation of the services of these contract 
employees with proper salaries, allowances and other facilities? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (DR SATYA NARAYAN JATIYA): 
(a) to (d) the Central Government have enacted the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 to protect the interests of contract 
labour engaged through contractors. It regulates the employment of contract 
labour in certain establishments and provides for  its abolition in certain 
circumstances. The Act and the rules made thereunder also provides for the 
regulation of conditions of work, payment of wages and other amenities 
relating to welfare and health of contract labour. 
The Contract Labour (Regulation and abolition) Central Rules, 1971 
provides that the rates of wages payable to the workmen of the contractor 
shall not be less than the rates prescribed under the Minimum Wages Act, 
1948 for such employment where applicable and where the rates have been 
fixed by agreement, settlement or award, not less titan the rates so fixed. In 
case, where the workman employed by the contractor performs the same or 
similar kind of work as the workmen directly employed by the p rincipal 
employer of the establishment, the wa ge rates, holidays, hours of work and 
other conditions of service of the workmen of the contractor shall be the same 
as applicable to the workmen directly employed by the principal employer of 
the establishment on the same or similar kind of work. In other  cases, the 
wage rates, holidays, hours of work and conditions of services of the 
workmen of the contractor shall be such as may be specified in this behalf by 
the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central). The data relating to payment of 
remuneration to contrac t workers by Central Public Sector Undertakings is 
not maintained centrally. However, complaints brought to the notice of the 
government regarding payment of less 
24 

[27 April, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
remuneration and pitiable conditions of contract labour are dealt with and 
appropriate action taken under the provisions of the Act and the rules. 
The Act does not provide for absorption of such labour on regular basis. 
In the aftermath of the judgement of the Supreme Court in Air India Statutory 
Corporations and O thers Vs. United Labour Union and Others, however, the 
establishments engaging contract labour are under statutory obligation to 
absorb contract labourers on regular basis wherever the "appropriate 
Government' by way of notification under section 10 of the  Contract Labour 
(Regulation and abolition) Act, 1970 have prohibited employment of contract 
labour in any job/work/ process in the establishment. The criteria to be 
adopted for absorption of such contract labour on regular basis as per the 
judgement will be the duration of work, number of employees working on the 
job etc. In case of retrenchment due to excess staff, the principle of "last 
come, first go' will be applied subject to reappointment as and when vacancy 
arises. 
The judgement of Hon' ble Supreme Court dated 6.12.96 in the case of 
Air India Statutory Corporations and Others Vs. United Labour Union and 
Others is the established law under Article 141 of the Constitution. It was 
published in 1997 LLR 288 and AIR 1997 SC 645. The implications of the 
judgement were examined in consultation with the Ministry of Law, Justice 
and Company Affairs and directions were issued to the emforcement agency 
of the Ministry of Labour to strictly implement the judgement in its letter and 
spirit.

Water wheel Turbine 
*477.  SHRI J.CHITHARANJAN: 
SHRI GAYA SINGH: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to a news -item 
appearing in the Economic Times, Delhi Edition, dated 12th March, 2000, 
under the caption "pump up the Volume" legarding the invention of a water 
wheel turbine that runs without fuel or electricity, by a UP farmer; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have any plan to help this inventor to start 
commercial production of this water wheel turbine; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SUNDAR LAL 
PATWA): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. A water wheel turbine has been developed by 
Shri Mangal Singh a farmer of village Bhailonilodh from district Lalitpur 
(UP). He also sought financial assistance from the Council for Ad vancement 
of Peoples' Action and Rural Technology (CAPART) under the Ministry of 
Rural Area & Employment, Govt. of India. The Water Wheel Turbine 
operates centrifugal pump(s), which can lift upto about 36 litres of water per 
second at 6.5 cm delivery head utilizing the hydrostatic energy of water by 
creating 1.8 meter water head using simple check dam in a flowing river or 
nala. The water current created pushes the paddles of the water wheel and 
rotates the wheel around its shaft, thus generating mechanical  power which is 
utilised to operate centrifugal pump(s). 
On the request of CAPART this water wheel turbine pump was 
inspected and assessed by the Scientists of Central Institute of Agricultural 
Engineering (CIAE), Bhopal during 1987 and in 1989. The perfor mance of 
the pump was found to be satisfactory although further refinements in the 
pump were recommended. It is learnt that Shri Mangal Singh has since 
obtained a patent of his water wheel turbine pump. It has been presented to 
International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) of Untied Nations in 
Rome who estimated system cost about Rs. 5.0 lakhs (at the price level of 
1998). Shri Mangal Singh wants that these be manufactured and installed for 
the benefit of the farmers. 
37 

RAJYA SABHA [27 April, 2000] 
(c) Since Shri Mangal Singh has already taken a patent on his invention, 
he may get the pump manufactured by some manufacturers for 
commercialisation, utilising the funds available from financial Institutions/ 
Banks for such help. 
(d) Not applicable.

(c) the reasons for this decline and the estimated rate likely to be gained 
in the first decade of 21st century? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
AGRICULTURE (SHRI SBPBK SATYANARAYANA RAO): (a) and (b) 
The annual compound growth rates of agriculture production during the 
decade of 80's and 90's have been 3.72% and 2.21% per annum respectively.  
(c) The deceleration in growth rate of production of agr icultural crops 
taken as a group is mainly on account of deceleration in the rate of growth of 
yield rates. 
The growth rate of production of agricultural crops depends upon a 
large number of factors such as agro -climatic conditions, performance of 
monsoon, timely application of seeds, fertilizers, managerial abilities of 
farmers, level of investment etc. Therefore, it is not possible to estimate at this 
stage, gain in growth rate in the first decade of 21st century. However, to 
increase production and produ ctivity and thus growth rate of agricultural 
crops in the country, the Government is implementing centrally sponsored 
Integrated Cereal Development Programmes in rice/wheat/coarse cereals 
Based Cropping System Area, National Pulses Development Project etc.  
Under these programmes/project, incentives are provided to farmers for use of 
high yielding varieties of seeds, application of integrated pest management, 
propagation of scientific water management including micro irrigation and 
use of improved farm imple ments. Research is also being continuously 
undertaken to develop improved technologies so as to enhance the 
productivity and production of foodgrains in India. Field demonstrations on 
farmers' holdings including training of farmers and farm labourers is be ing 
organised for effective transfer of technology.

productivity of Coffee, Tea, Rubber and Coconut are given below: 
Coffee: The Coffee Board implements programmes for intensive 
cultivation, replanting, quali ty improvement and water augmentation. The 
Board has also been providing necessary support in the form of agricultural 
research, extension, arrangement of credit and finance and other necessary 
back up supports like supply of coffee seeds for planting purposes. The

1996 Kg. / ha. in 1998. 
Rubber: The Rubber Board is making available financial and technical 
assistance for new planting and replanting with improved varieties, 
production and distribution of high yielding planting materials to growers, 
rendering adviso ry, extension and training service; encouraging group 
processing and marketing among small holders, undertaking research on 
cultivation, production and processing of rubber. A World Bank assisted 
Rubber Project is also under implementation from 1993- 94 to enhance 
production and improve quality of

programmes with an outlay of Rs. 105.00 crores during 9th Plan, which inter -
alia, include Production and distribution of quality planting material; Area 
expansion; Integrated farming in coconut holdings for productivity 
improvement; Control of leaf eating caterpillars; and promotion of product

3569. SHRI EDU ARDO FALEIRO: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that several countries are phasing out nuclear 
power stations after the Chernobyl and Three Mile incidents apart from 
scores of other lesser known incidents and health hazards caused to workers 
and nearby populations; 
(b) whether Government are aware that several recent studies have 
established the highly dangerous effects of low level nuclear radiation; and  
(c) if so, reaction of Government thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTM ENT OF ATOMIC 
ENERGY (SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) Electricity generation 
by Nuclear Energy in the world increased by about 26% during the period 
1990— 99 as per information available. Although there has been slowing 
down in nuclear power capacity additi on in U.S.A., Canada and Western 
Europe, this is to be looked at in the context of their self -sufficiency in 
meeting the electricity demand with a high level of per capita electricity 
consumption, stagnant population growth as well as easy access to other 
energy sources. It cannot be attributed to safety reasons. Safety in Nuclear 
Power Plants are getting continously upgraded world over to meet emerging 
concerns from time to time including lessons learnt from Chernobyl and 
Three Mile Island Accident. The nu clear capacity addition is now centered in 
Asia. 
A study, based on International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) 
documents indicates that between the period 1990 to 1997 48 Nuclear Power 
Reactors were connected to the grid and as of the end of 1998,36 Nuclear 
Power Reactors with a net capacity of 27536 MWe are reported to be under 
construction. About 16% of the world electricity needs are being met through 
nuclear power reactors. 
(b) and (c) Studies on the biological effects of Nuclear Radiation have 
been in pr ogress in several research institutions for many decades. These 
studies have been analysed and summarised by the United Nations Scientific 
Committee on the effects of Atomic Radiation. Based on these studies, the 
International Commission on Radiological Pr otection — a specialist 
organisation — makes periodic recommendations on the safe use of radiation. 
In line with these recommndations, the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board 
issues appropriate safely directives to regurlate radiation exposure to radiation 
workers and members of the public in India.

National Wage Policy for Bidi Labourers 
3608. MISS. MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of LABOUR be  
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government will make a National Policy for Bidi 
Labourers so that they may get equal wages all over the country; 
(b) whether Government will take necessary steps to ensure that the 
Bidi magnates do not shift their Bidi manufacturing units to States having 
lower wages for Bidi making thereby rendering lakhs of bidi labourers 
without employment and on the verge of starvation in Madhya Pradesh; and

residential accommodation for Bidi labourers in Mahdya Pradesh? 
112 

[27 April, 2000]                     RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT (SHRI MUNI LALL): (a) and (b) The Government has 
examined the issue of a National Wage Policy which has been discussed on 
many occasions in different fora. Since fixation of wages depends on a 
number of factors like local conditions, cost of living and paying capacity, 
which varies from State to State and from Industry to Industry, it has not been 
found feasible to maintain uniformity in wages all over the country. The 
Indian Labour Conference, held in November 1985 express ed that 'Till such 
time a national wage is feasible, it would be desirable to have regional 
minimum wages in regard to which the Central Government may lay down 
the guidelines. The minimum wages should be revised at regular periodicity 
and should be linked with rise in the cost of living." Accordingly, the 
Government issued guidelines in July, 87 for setting up of Regional Minimum 
Wages Advisory Committees. These Committees renamed subsequently as 
Regional Labour Ministers' Conferences, made a number of recommendations 
which include reduction in disparities in minimum wages in different states of 
a region, setting up of Inter -State Coordination Council and consultation with 
neighbourig States while fixing/ revising minimum wages. 
In the absence of a National  Wage Policy, the Central Government 
introduced National Floor Level Minimum Wage of Rs. 35/ - per day in 1996 
based on the recommendations of the National Commission on Rural Labour 
in 1991 and subsequent increase in price level. The Floor Level Minimum 
Wage was further enhanced to Rs. 40/- per day in August, 1998 when Hon'ble 
Prime Minister wrote to all the State Governments/Union Territories 
requesting them to ensure that minimum wages are not paid below Rs. 40/ - 
per day for any scheduled employment. It h as been further increased to Rs. 
45/- per day due to increase in the Consumer Price Index Number.

article 243 (g) to endow the Panchayats with such powers and authorities, as 
may be necessary, to enable them to function as institutions of self -
government. Even today most of the States are not giving the necessary 
powers to the Panchayats. Though they are not given the powers, they are the 
only approachable institutions by the poorest of the poor and those who are 
living in rural areas. The States are not giving the powers to the Panchayats 
and they are helpless. They can exercise powers only when th ey are given .to 
them. Now, they are compelled to beg those who are having powers. If the 
functioning of the Gram Panchayats are undermined, the roots of our 
democracy will be shaken. This is my submission to the House. 
Sir, the Tenth Finance Commission ha d taken into consideration the 
pathetic financial conditions of Gram Panchayats and was kind enough to 
make some recommendations. I quote from the recommendations: 
"We are making an ad hoc provision of Rs. 100 per capita 
of rural population. For all States  the figures are indicated 
at Annexure XI. This amount should be distributed amongst 
the panchayati raj institutions, over and above their due, by 
way of their share of the assigned taxes, duties, tolls, fees, 
transferred activity-related budgets and 
151 

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 APRIL, 2000] 
grants. Even in those States which are not required to have 
panchayats, as envisaged in the 73rd amendment of the 
Constitution, the additional amounts would be required to 
be given to supplement the resources of similar local level 
representative bodies." 
According to this recommendation, all the States together should get 
from the Central Government an amount of Rs. 4,380.93 crores at the rate of 
Rs. 1,095 crores per year from 1996- 97 onwards, that is, for four years. The 
share of Andhra Pradesh for these four years is Rs. 351 crores at the rate of 
87.75 crores per year. The Central Government was kind enough to release 
the share of Andhra Pradesh for 1996 -97 and 1997- 98, but the share of Rs. 
175.5 crores for 1998- 99 and 1999- 2000 has not been released till date. 
Recently, a delegation from Andhra Pradesh came to Delhi and met our 
Minister of Rural Development, Mr. Sunderlal Patwa, and the Minister 
promised them to release the share of Andhra Pradesh for these two years by 
31st March, 2000. But, I am sorry to say that that amount has not been 
released till today. There are 21,934 Sarpanches in Andhra Pradesh. They are 
agitating. A week ago a delegation came here to request the Central 
Government to release the funds. Sir, I appeal, through you, to the hon. 
Finance Minister and the hon. Minister of Rural Development to release 
immediately the share of Andhra Pradesh for the years 1998 -99 and 1999-
2000, that is, an amount of Rs. 175.5 crores. I believe the same thing is 
happening in the case of other States also. The entire amount recommended 
by the Tenth Finance Commission should be released keeping in view the 
necessity of strengthening the functioning of the Gram Panchayats. 
Problems being faced by Telephone users' allottees and non attending of 
complaints by Telecom authorities in Time 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh) : Thank you, 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, for giving me this opportunity. The telephone connections 
have increased manifold in the country, particularly in Hyderabad. As a 
measure to face, the stiff competition from the private sector, the Telecom 
Department has been making efforts to increase connections in Hyderabad. 
With this, however, the problems of the consumers have also increased. 
Though new schemes were announc ed and the capacity of the exchanges has 
been increased, the consumers are 
152 

[ 27 APRIL, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
not getting the connections in time. The consumers are waiting for 
connections for months together. For example, the setting up of a new 
exchange in Uppahiru of Krishna district was announced and a building was 
constructed many' months ago. Still, it has not been opened and the people 
are awaiting connections. In Hyderabad, many people got the wiring done 
and also got the instruments, but connection was not given for months 
together. This is a peculiar situation with the Telecom Department. If we ask 
from a private company like Tata, in Hyderabad, they will give the 
connection the very next day. When will the Telecom Department become so 
prompt? Alth ough the Telecom Department had brought out the 
advertisement that within 24 hours, the complaints will be attended to; and 
within 25 days of the request shifting of phone will be done, yet these are 
delayed for days and months. I want the Government to ta ke necessary action 
and ensure better and prompt facilities to the consumers; otherwise the day is 
not far off when the private sector will overtake the Telecom Department.  
Thank you, Sir.

Non-Holding of Panchayat elections by State Governments every 
five years 
SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD (Bihar): Sir, I am extremely 
grateful to you for giving me the opportunity to make my Special Mention. 
Sir, I am raising a matter of great importance, namely, the complete crippl ing 
effect on the functioning of the local bodies and gram panchayats in the 
country, on account of non -holding of elections. Sir, as you are aware, article 
40 of the Constitution says "The State shall take steps to organise village 
panchayats and endow them with such powers and authority as may be 
necessary to enable them to function as units of self -government." Sir, the 
73rd Amendment was made which led to far -reaching changes in article 243 
which clearly said " Every Panchayat, unless sooner dissolved u nder any law 
for the time being in force, shall continue for five years from the date 
appointed for its first meeting and no longer." The question of the Tenth 
Finance Commission has already been raised by my hon. friend, Mr. Reddy, I 
do not want to repeat that. But, Sir, that is a very serious question. As a result 
of these amendments to the Constitution, in many States, like Madhya 
Pradesh and others, local bodies are functioning .   But in other States, no 
election, either in respect of gram 
153 

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 APRIL, 2000] 
panchayat or local bodies, has been held. I would particularly refer to my own 
State of Bihar where, since 1978, no election, either of gram panchayats or of 
municipality has been held. Sir, it is a very serious matter since there is  a 
judicial order of the High Court to hold the elections to gram panchayats and 
local bodies. The people are being denied of their right to self -governance. 
Besides, Sir, the people of the State of Bihar are also being denied of. the 
funds because, as per  the Tenth Finance Commission's recommendations, the 
money is to be released only to the panchayats and local bodies which are 
functional. We gather that as much as Rs. 400 crores is being lost every year 
by these municipal bodies and gram panchayats on account of the non-holding 
of elections. It is a very serious matter. It is a matter which ought to be taken 
notice of. I would request through you, Sir, the Government to kindly ensure 
that the complete case of violation of the constitutional mandate ought not to 
be resorted to and the people of Bihar must be given the opportunity, at the 
earliest, of self-Government. Thank you, Sir.

Telecast of car festival of Puri on Doordarshan 
DR. M.N. DAS (Orissa): Mr. Chairma n, Sir, I am making a 
submission regarding live telecast of the Car Festival of Lord Jagannath in 
Puri. This is one of the rarest of the rare festivals in India. To participate in 
this festival, thousands and thousands of people come from various parts of 
the country. Millions of people all over the world, not only millions in India 
but also outside India, would like to see this' festival on Doordarshan. For the 
last several years, Doordarshan has been covering the Car Festival live. But 
we are shocked to h ear that this year the Government has decided not to 
telecast the Car festival live. Sir, when I refer to Lord Jagannath, let me say 
for the kind information of the hon. Members that this famous deity is not 
specifically or particularly regarded as a Hindu  deity. Originally Lord 
Jagannath was the deity of the most primitive tribal people living in dense 
forests. 
But with the Aryan migration to ancient Kalinga, i.e. modern Orissa, 
a King brought the deity from the forest and placed it at Puri. From that time , 
the descendents of the tribals are still the chief priests of the Lord and they 
perform all the religious duties and rites inside the temple. When Lord 
Buddha attained holy Nirvana, his Holy Tooth was brought to Puri of Kalinga 
by a Buddhist monk, Kshema thera, who handed it over to the King of 
Kalinga. Still the tradition holds, and the firm faith of the people is, that the 
Holy Tooth of Buddha is kept in the Navipadma of Jagannath and the 
Buddhist influence is so evident that there is no caste system. In Puri, the 
mahaprasada of Lord Jagannath is taken by the brahmins and the chandalas, 
together, from the same plate. The present great temple was built by 
Chodagangade in the 11th century. The finest bhajans on Lord Jagannath 
come    from    a   Muslim    poet    named    Sal   Beg    and    the    most 
156 

[ 27 APRIL, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
modern devotees of Lord Jagannath happen to be thousands of Christians of 
USA, of England, who have become members of ISKCON. One would find 
the Christians of ISKCON in the Car Festival of Lord Jagannath at Puri, in 
front of the chariots, praying and dancing, playing the musical instruments 
and singing bhajans in melodious voice. About a Millions of people gather 
there, but millions who cannot come would like to see the festival on 
Doordarshan. So, I would appeal to the Government that the live telecast of 
the Car Festival be shown as in previous years. I do not know why they 
should decide not to telecast it live this year. It is my appeal through you, Sir, 
to the Government to present a live Telecast of the festival. 
Thank you. 
SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA (Orissa): Mr. Chairman, Sir, it 
has been published in a Delhi newspaper 'Samaj' that the Central Government 
has denied permission for live telecast of the Car Festival; also, th ey are not 
releasing money which is required for the Rath Yatra. Mr Chairman; Sir, the 
annual Car Festival of Lord Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra -  the Trinity 
- falls this year on 3rd July. This is the only occasion during a year when the 
deities are brought out of the temple and placed on their respective chariots 
and are pulled to a temple complex some four kilometres away where they are 
housed for nine days and taken back to the temple. The mythology - bound 
Rath Yatra is an event where a million people gather from all over the country 
and even from outside. Thousands of people from the West, particularly 
ISKCON members, who do not have access inside the temple benefit by 
seeing the deities. All India Radio has been giving running commentary of the 
event for the last at least forty years. When the facility of direct telecast on the 
television developed, Doordarshan has, for more than five years, brought the 
celebration to the viewers throughout the country. -Hindus believe that by 
seeing the Lord on t he Chariot, man escapes the birth cycle. Lord Jagannath 
has generated a powerful cementing force. Though non -Hindus have no 
access inside the temple, they are allowed darshan and even the facility of 
embracing the Lord on this occasion. Jagannath is the Lo rd of the world, as 
the name itself indicates. Every Oriya - whether a Hindu or not is proud of the 
Lord and looks for the great day to arrive. The Vaishnavs all over India 
anxiously wait to see the direct telecast of the ceremonies connected with the 
festival Perhaps, on a modest estimate, the number of viewers would be about 
five 
157 

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 APRIL, 2000] 
crores. The people of Orissa are shocked to learn that this year, Doordarshan 
does not intend to have a direct telecast of the event. This will adversely 
affect the pride of Orissa and injure the sentiments of the people. The cult of 
Jagannath, the traditional and mythological events connected with the Lord, 
transcend any particular religion and bring the people together. Instead of 
taking advantage of this great cementing influence, Doordarshan should not 
make the mistake of abandoning the live telecast of the event. We, all the 
Members of Parliament from Orissa, urge upon the government through you 
to kindly release the necessary financial assis tance for the Lord Jagannath 
Chariot Festival and also pass necessary orders for the live telecast of the 
festival on 3rd July, 2000.  Thank you. 
SHRI M. VENKAIAH NAIDU (Karnataka) : Sir, I rise to associate

taking up the economic issues -has quite rightly sakl that the Government 
ought to build a consensus in regard to the question of econo mic reforms. I 
totally accept that. Indeed, the Government recognises that, in a field as

such that there ought to be a consensus and one approach in this regard, and 
partisan politics, to the extent possible, in ah assembly which is essentially 
political, should be put asid e for larger purposes. Therefore, the advice of the 
hon. Leader of the Opposition that the Government should endeavour to 
create a consensus in this regard is entirely acceptable to the Government. We 
will make efforts to do so. The Prime Minister has poin ted out, while

require a national consensus. In that context., I refer to the second major issue,

governing in one part of India or the other. There fore, it is necessary for me to

Government has the responsibility to manage the Central finances. That is not 
possible, unless the finances of the States are also equally healthy.

Commission has given its recommendations. This Government has held 
meetings of the National D evelopment Council, taken decisions and acted in 
accordance with the recommendations of the Finance Commission. The

Government in discharge of its responsibility, and keeping in mind fiscal

India appealed this before the appellate body of the W.T.O. The 
appellate body, in its report on 23rd August, 1999, upheld the findings of the 
panel and recommended that the Disputes Settlement Body of the W.T.O. 
request India to bring its balance of payments restrictions into conformity 
with its obligation under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. The 
Disputes Settlement Body adopted these recommendations in September, 
1999. India indicated its intention to comply with the rulings and 
recommendations of the Disputes Settlement Body and also indicated that it 
required more than the normal 15 -month period for the implementation and 
we wanted a definition of what in WTO terms is called R.P.T. (Reasonable 
Period of Time). This was not acceptable to the U.S.A and, when there is a 
dispute between the parties like this, a reaso nable period of time is to be 
determined either by a bilateral agreement between the contesting parties or 
through an arbitrator. The arbitrator, normally, does not provide for more than 
15 months. After bilateral discussions to determine the time period, India and 
the U.S. signed a bi -lateral agreement on 28th December, 1999 Under this 
agreement, the final reasonable period of time will expire on 1st April, 2000. 
Out of the 1429 tariff lines, at the eight digit -level, on which Quantitative 
Restrictions were maintained by India on the grounds of balance of payments, 
under direct signing of the agreement, 714 items were removed on 1st April, 
2000 and the balance 715 by 1st April, 2001. As India has removed 
Quantitative Restrictions on 714, coinciding with the  Annual Exim Policy for 
2000-01, following the final expiry of the reasonable period of time, India 
would have to use the instrument of tariffs to provide protection to domestic 
industry.

fashion that is a consequence of fully deliberating it and, out of that 
deliberation, working out all that requires to be done. 
Hence, a Committee of Ministers has been formed. Dr. Karan Singh 
is quite right if he points out that this Committee of Ministers, by itself, will 
not suffice. All that I can urge him to see is this. The Prim e Minister, in his 
wisdom, has appointed these Ministers because he feels that if there is ' the 
overall responsibility of these Ministers, then, the recommendations and the 
deliberations and determinations that these Ministers will make, will, 
certainly, be only after they have fully established, if needed sub -committees, 
and involved all the specialists that are to be involved. Only then will they 
come forward with a report. I can only urge him to reflect on this or to 
comment on this after he sees its ac tion, at least for the first two or three 
times. We will, certainly, benefit if any hon. Member here in this House or in 
the other House has views in regard to the 
189 

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 APRIL, 2000] 
management of security, he will get an opportunity so tha t the deliberations 
of this Committee are as broad -based, as truthful, as all -encompassing, as 
possible in the circumstances. 
Dr. Karan Singh also mentioned about the State of Jammu and 
Kashmir. It is correct that there are three dimensions --the internatio nal, the 
internal and specific to Jammu and Kashmir, the regional. I can assure the 
hon. Member on the international dimension. I would like to share with the 
House what I said in the U.N. General Assembly. We do not treat that the 
Indian State of Jammu and Kashmir is what our western neighbour Pakistan, 
sometimes, would like to call either 'unfinished agenda' or the 'core issue'. 
The Indian State of Jammu and Kashmir is not the core issue between India 
and Pakistan. Jammu and Kashmir is at the core of the Indian nation only. 
This is a statement that has been made by this Government in the U.N. 
General Assembly. It has been made, for the first time, last year. This is how 
the Government approaches this responsibility. 
So far as regionally maintaining the peculiar diversity of the State 
of Jammu and Kashmir is concerned, let me assure the hon. Member and all 
other Members that may have concerns in this regard, that the sheer beauty 
and vividity of Jammu and Kashmir shall not be permitted even to be dented, 
leave alone suffer. 
Mr. Vice-Chairman, you have been very generous in giving me time. 
I share with all hon. Members the sense of "a nation on the move". It is a 
nation on the move. As the Prime Minister has said, 60 per cent of the nation 
being less than 35 years old, it is a young nation. And, when the young nation 
of ours is on the move, we appeal to all hon. Members that the only manner in 
which we can facilitate the movement of this great nation is through 
consensus. The consensus aims at rapid development , balanced and 
harmonious development. Our commitment is for economic reforms for all, 
economic reforms with a human face. The development is for all and the 
development is not for a few or some only. Let us attempt at this, put aside 
small contentions, petty disputations. Do, by all means, score points against us 
in the Government. But, in the process of scoring points against us in the 
Government, take care, and aim off sufficiently, that we do not 
simultaneously, even unwittingly, score points against th is young India. This 
assembly, Mr. Vice- Chairman, is for debate and discourse. Through that 
debate and discourse, this young India that is on the move seeks 
190 

[ 27 APRIL, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
direction. Of course, it is the Government's responsibility to p rovide 
direction. But it is the collective responsibility of the whole House to give the 
sense of direction and leadership. 
And it is towards providing that sense collectively that I invite all 
Members to join step with us in this great, exciting and all inspiring adventure 
of leading this young India to its true destiny. Such, Sir, indeed is our 
bounden duty; such a Government, we believe, is both our raj and dharma, to 
which we are bound. Therefore, I appeal to all Members, while thanking the 
Mover of the  resolution, to share with us in expressing our gratitude to hon. 
the President. 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE : Sir, I would like to seek 
clarifications from the hon. Minister on three points. While responding to the 
issue of the Constitutional Review, the hon. M inister has referred to the 39th 
Amendment, and tried to build up a case that certain measures are required to 
be reviewed. But he has conveniently forgotten that the 39th Amendment is 
no longer a part of,the Indian Constitution today. It was replaced by t he 44th 
Amendment. He might equally recollect that the Janata Party piloted the 44th 
Amendment, while sitting on the Treasury Benches, myself sitting on this 
side of the House, and Shri Kamlapati Tripathi was occupying the place of 
Dr. Manmohan Singh. We e xtended our wholehearted support to pass that 
Amendment. Otherwise, with sixteen Members in this House, you could not 
have carried a Constitutional Amendment. This is precisely the point. We 
wanted to know, please tell us, which article, which part, which section you 
want to amend. You got a limited mandate. We will go with you. Let us know 
what amendments you want, and for what purpose. In this connection, may I 
most respectfully submit that we never believe in the basic structure of the 
Constitution. We believe that the Parliament is omnipotent, It should have all 
powers to amend any part of the Constitution. That is the rationale behind 
injecting the doctrine of constituent power of Parliament, by amending article 
368, inserting clause (1) in article 368.  If you want to pass on, that we believe 
in the basic structure and the basic structure is not going to be altered because 
nobody knows what the basic structure is, the Supreme Court is unfolding, 
and they have not exhaustively codified it. The second poin t on which I 
would like to seek clarification from him is that he has given three reasons 
why dialogue cannot be resumed with Pakistan. One reason is: Pakistan's 
Kandhar misadventure, Kargil and military coup. May I know from the hon. 
191 

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 APRIL, 2000] 
Minister whether it is the first military coup in Pakistan? What happened in 
1958? What happened in 1978? Is it not a fact that out of 53 years of its 
existence, for as many as 25 years, Pakistan was under military regime? But 
still we had dialogues, still we had talks. It is not that Kargil is the only armed 
conflict with Pakistan. We had it in 1948, we had it in 1965 and we had it in 
1971. It is not for the first time that there was hijacking in Kandhar. In 1974, 
hijacking took place in Lahore where the Indian Airlines aircraft was burnt. In 
1980 again, it happened, in 1984 it happened. Therefore, all these three 
reasons which you have given as to why a dialogue cannot be resumed with 
Pakistan, Mr. Minister, all these reasons existed before t he Lahore 
Declaration, and still, we had to deal with them. We cannot erase the very 
basic fact... (Interruptions) Mr. B.P. Singhal please do not disturb me. I did 
not disturb the Minister. I listened to him with rapt attention. These are the 
clarifications I am trying to have from the Minister and the Minister is 
competent enough to reply to my clarifications. 
We have been repeatedly saying from this side that, 'Yes, there is 
need for reducing expenditure, but please open a dialogue. Please try to build 
up a consensus and take the lead.' Can you deal with subsidies on fertilisers, 
food and kerosene in this piecemeal manner? If, in two years, you had floated 
a paper, or, revised Mr. Chidambaram's paper, or, started a dialogue with the 
political parties, then,  by this time, you could have come to a consensus. It 
would have helped you, or, whoever was in the Government, to carry on. 
Surely, one will agree that 16 to 17 per cent of the GDP cannot go towards 
subsidies. But, certainly, we would not like the food su bsidy to be cut because 
it is closely linked with our food security. The basic point is, why don't you 
have an integrated, comprehensive, approach to this issue. Yes; you have 
appointed an Expenditure Commission. But like in the case of Constitution 
review, your primary concern should be Parliament; so, you are trying to 
stage Hamlet without the Prince of Denmark. You are trying to have the 
Constitution reviewed by experts. Yes; they are very respectable persons. But 
what would happen ultimately? It would r emain a thesis paper and it will 
never be truly reflective, unless you involve the people sitting in this House 
and that House. 
My third point is: I entirely agree with you that the Rs. 75,000/- crore 
deficit by the States cannot be carried on. You have adv ised, if I have heard 
you correctly, that they should avoid competitive populism.    But

would it not be equally applicable to the Federal Government? After all, ours

SHRI JASWANT SINGH: The other economic point was raised by 
Shri Pranab Mukherjee which related to Expenditure Commission, and you 
advocated with which I agree. It is not enough to just simply appoint an 
Expenditure Commission. Is it only the responsibility of the State and not the 
responsibility of the Union?    No, Sir.    There should be equal 
201 

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 APRIL, 2000] 
responsibility. We share the responsibility. After all, the Union Government 
cannot function as a separate and apart and autonomous; autonomous in a 
functional sense, autonomous not in a consequential sense. The consequences 
of what we do at the Centre and what we do in the States are closely 
interrelated; they are inseparable; they are interwoven together. And if we 
have an illusion that the States can perform autonomously, without 
simultaneously the Centre also doing so, it is an illusion. Therefore, in that 
sense, I share that, Yes, we have a joint responsibility. Ought we to consult 
each other? With out any doubt whatsoever, we must consult each other 
because reduction of expenditure is a collective responsibility. I can assure 
you on behalf of the Government that there is no doubt that my distinguished 
colleague, the Finance Minister, will initiate a suitable dialogue with everyone 
concerned at the appropriate time. 
You did not do me justice, Sir, after all that I had said; I had offered 
three reasons for having the position that the Government has in regard to 
resumption of dialogue with Pakistan. No, Sir, I cited incidents. The 
aggression in Kargil is a consequence. It was not simply a violation of the 
political boundary and territory of India. It was, without any doubt 
whatsoever, a transgression on the territory and the trust also. Kargil or 
Kandahar or the military coup, are not by themselves the causes. These are 
not the conditions. They are incidents. What I have said, what I have said 
today also, not as pre -conditions, but as essential ingredients for the creation 
of a suitable climate; we need to have our Western neighbour, Pakistan, abjure 
violence, reaffirm the essentials of bilateral relations, which are, after all, the 
Shimla Agreement, the treaty documents and the Lahore Declaration. Why? 
Because, the Chief Executive has recently said, and he repeated, that he does 
not believe in these. We assert that cross -border terrorism must cease. Why? 
Because you cannot simultaneously engage in cross -border terrorism, put a 
pistol to my head and say, "Now, talk to me". Stopping cross -border 
terrorism, abjuring violence, are not conditions. The dialogue process that was 
set in motion by India has been fractured, has been interrupted. Those who 
have fractured or interrupted it, the onus is on them to recreate the conditions 
so that the process can be resumed. I did not cite those three.

has this not been done?    It is the prerogative of the hon. Prune
