also....(Interruptions).... Any kind of planning or budgetting has no meaning 
if the correlation among the three is not established. Huge amounts are 
allotted to be kept unutilised by the State Government.   We are entitled 
213 

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 APRIL, 2000] 
to know as to which are the States which are fortunat e enough to get these 
amounts. At least, I presume that there has been no politics involved in this 
because, ultimately, if the unutilised amount is lying with the State 
Governments, it can be used as a kind of ways -and-means advance. The 
Government of India seems to be having plenty of money. They are allowing 
this money to be lying unutilised with the State Governments. And, without 
asking for the utilisation certificates every year, grants are being released. So, I 
won't be wrong if I have to say that yo u seem to be having plenty of money 
with which you would like to help the State Governments in this manner. That 
is why I am very particular to find out which are the . fortunate States where 
huge amounts are lying unutilised so that we may be convinced th at there is 
nothing hanky-panky and that you are not trying to play politics with some of 
the State Governments. 
There is another aspect. In fact, I would like to quote from a 
Standing Committee report. This is not my innovation. "In fact, the tendency 
is drastically to cut the Plan expenditure and increase the amount or adjust the 
amount against non -Plan." In this respect, I would like to know one thing 
from the hon. Minister. I hope they are following the guidelines given by the 
Finance Commission and no committed expenditure is being charged to these 
Plan schemes. The Plan schemes are being reduced and the Non -Plan amount 
are being increased. I would be very happy if my information is wrong. But I 
have seen in some other Departments where I am the Chairma n of the 
Standing Committee. They have been openly violating everything. The 
Expenditure Secretary appeared before us as a witness and he told us the head 
under which so much amount has been kept for Committee expenditure. But 
no Department bothers about i t and they are just charging all the Plan 
schemes. Every year, the Plan amount is getting reduced and the Non -Plan 
amount is on the increase, and that is why, the Standing Committee was 
pleased to recommend to the Government, "you had better appoint some 
expert group which should decide as to what should be the proportion 
between the Plan and Non-  Plan schemes." If the Non - Plan schemes are 
going to take over the Plan schemes, then, of course, there is hardly any 
amount left for any kind of development in this respect. If I have to quote the 
trend of expenditure from the Demands for Grants for the year 1998- 99 -this 
is the report of the Standing Committee on Agriculture - you will find that the 
total amount available for the Eighth Plan was Rs: One thousand    crores. ' 
The 
214 

[ 27 APRIL, 2000]   RAJYA SABHA 
amount which they have been alloted during the Eighth Plan, was of Rs. 
100000 crores, at the BE stage, was Rs. 90062 crores, at the RE stage, it came 
down to Rs. 67,961 crores, and the actual expenditur e was Rs. 56470 crores. 
What a tremendous change! Out of the the entire Plan provision, not even half 
the amount has been spent. I do not know how the Department can possibly 
ask for any more allocation to be given when we know that at the RE stage, it 
was getting reduced and the actual amount that you were able to spend was 
much less. What is the justification for this asking more money? I do not 
think that you can get away like this. For years together, this has been 
happening. I have seen it during 1998 -99, I have seen it during 1999 -  2000 
also. In respect of the Ninth Plan expenditure, in the very first year, I find that 
the same kind of story has been repeated. What is the physical achievement? 
When I compare the foodgrains production from 1993- 94 to 1996- 97, I find 
that it was 184.3 million tonnes, 191.5 million tonnes, 180.4 million tonnes, 
199.3 million tronnes, and for the first year of the Ninth Plan, the target was 
200 million tonnes, the estimated production is going to be 194 million 
tonnes. These are the figures which, in fact, speak for themselves that there is 
no corelationship between the amount of production that you have and the 
amount of money that has been allotted to you. You have to have some kind 
of a relationship and you owe some kind of explanation to the Parliament as 
to why you were not able to spend the money. Might be, I have not dealt with 
one aspect, which I would like to remind the hon. Minister. I was also the 
Finance Minister and I used to insist that schemes which are enteri ng into the 
Budget, they have to be formally approved by every Department concerned. 
But now I find that everybody is happy. You just announce and it gets into 
the Budget. 
Thereafter, for three years, you were not able to take any decision 
about the details as to what you propose to do under that scheme. That is why 
I am saying that budgeting has lost its importance. Budgeting has no meaning 
left for you. You are happy to announce the scheme and, thereafter, you leave 
it. Whenever you find that you are in d ifficulty, you always blame the State 
Government, saying the State Government has not done this and that. I don't 
think that by blaming each other, we can find an escape route.. Ultimately, in 
the next decade, our population is going to be the highest. We are going to 
exceed China also. What is the total amount of food production that we will 
require? It should be, at least, doubled.   I 
215 

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 APRIL, 2000] 
forgot to tell you about the rate of growth. The rate of growth in agricultural 
production, as it is given to us, was about 2.6 per cent in the 8th Plan. On this 
basis, I doubt whether you would be able to double the agricultural 
production. Looking at the trend that we had in the 8th Plan, I think you will 
have to make special efforts in o rder to see that you are able to achieve the 
target of foodgrains production. The population is going to increase by about 
4 to 4.5 crore and you are thinking that by having an average growth in 
production of 4.5 per cent, you will be able to equalise the growth in 
population with the growth in production. That is the basis on which you are 
trying to have the details worked out. I have my own doubts and that is why I 
have frankly told you that I will be very happy if my Assam friends are 
proved wrong. 
The next point which I would like to specially emphasis is dry land 
agriculture. Small and marginal farmers have to inherit this land from their 
ancestral property. As a result of the honest implementation of the Land 
Ceiling Act, there are some States which have done some excellent work. 
And because of that, some small and marginal farmers have got some land. 
Now they are totally out of this national endeavour of food 
production. Why are they not given loans from the District Cooperative Banks 
in the initial stages? When the District Cooperative Banks don't give them 
loans, ultimately, they have to approach the moneylenders. And, in fact, the 
moneylenders are charging a high rate of interest. They have the muscle 
power and, if by any chance, he were to fail in r epayment - which he is bound 
to, because of the floods, drought and other natural calamities -then, the 
moneylender makes the life of that man miserable. That is one of the reasons 
as to why so many farmers have gone to the extent of committing suicide - 
suicide is not any kind of pleasure - and nobody comes to his rescue. I was 
surprised when one of the Ministers happened to say that some psychiatrist 
should be sent to find out if there is some abnormality in his brain. This is a 
very cruel sort of joke that you are playing on them. These poor people are, in 
fact, very honest. They are prepared to pay each paisa of that money, but if it 
goes beyond their limit, and if moneylenders harass them to such an extent, 
what else can you expect from these cultivator s? My request to you is, if you 
are really interested in doubling your production, then, you will have to 
encourage the involvement of these small and marginal farmers, and instead 
of reducing the subsidy, I think there is a good case for giving them good 
seeds, good fertilizers and good 
216 

[ 27 APRIL, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
pesticides.   Though it is obtained at a concessional rate, it is a question of 
investment in the land. 
If you don't invest in the land, you wouldn't automatically get the 
production that you expect. For this purpose, it is very necessary that you 
should seriously consider as to whether you can prepare a special scheme for 
the small and marginal farmers to bring them into the mainstream and to see 
that they increase their production. 
The ne xt point which I would like to touch is this. There are a 
number of Ministries which are also, in fact, involved in this. The other day I 
was curiously listening to the Commerce Minister. He was making a 
declaration that we had allowed the import of many items like food, oil seeds, 
milk, etc. He had announced that even milk and milk products would be 
allowed to be imported because of the WTO obligation. Very well, you have 
an obligation of WTO. In this context, it would be better, if I give some 
extracts from an interview given by Dr. Swaminathan to FRONTLINE. I am 
quoting from the FRONTLINE. This is the issue dated December 24, 1999. I 
will touch only two aspects, one is about the globalisation and its effects and 
the other is about the announcement made by  the Commerce Minister and its 
implications. I quote: 
"Globalisation, indicating the removal of economic policies which 
protect the vulnerable sections of society, has certainly led to 
growing inequity between nations and within nations The available 
data from the United Nations and the World Bank sources show that 
in the last 20 years the global domestic economic product has grown 
from about $ 10 trillion in 1980 to over $30 trillion now, an increase 
of almost three times. This money has largely gone to ab out 12 to 13 
countries, mostly industrialised. And in the poorer nations where 
some growth has taken place, most of the additional income has 
gone to the already well -to-do. Seven or eight years ago it was 
mentioned that one billion of the world's populati on was earning less 
than one dollar a day. Now this one billion has gone up to 1.3 
billion. And according to the Asian Development Bank, one in three 
Asians is poor and lives below the poverty line, earning less than one 
dollar a day. Most of the poor, 900 million people, live in our part of 
the world, South Asia and South-East Asia. 
217 

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 APRIL, 2000] 
Why has this happened? Growth has not been even and has been 
highly skewed in terms of countries and in terms of communities 
within the countries. " 
There are a number of other things which I would like to refer. 
"Although the World Food Summit in 1996 called for halving by 
2015 of the numbers of men, women and children going to bed 
hundgry, the Director -General of the FAO has said that the pos ition 
has worsened in many countries since 1996." 
Now, I will quote his statement about the list which was announced 
by the hon. Commerce Minister. Today also the Leader of the House was 
pleased to say that we had enough power in our hands. They may be thi nking 
that after allowing all these imports they can impose excise duty. I will come 
to that later. I am raising the same kind of issue. I quote: 
"Our Commerce Ministry's policy statement on import and export 
must have a livelihood impact statement. It has  a sobering influence, 
because then you start looking at what is really going to happen. For 
example, if India begins importing somuch of milk power and puts 
milk power on the OGL, what is going to happen to the National 
Dairy Development Board's efforts w hich over a long period time 
have led us to the first position in milk production in the world?" 
Because our people are very small producers. This is also true of 
many sectors - whether it is in the broad area of textiles which generates over 
60 million jobs in this country, or the dairy sector which gives to 8 crore or 10 
crore people in the rural areas additional livelihood through ownership of a 
cow or a buffalo. This is the decentralised system that we have adopted. And 
by just announcing this, if you get this milk power into this country, it is the 
end of the National Dairy Development Board. Our production process, by 
and large, still falls under the small- scale sector and, today, poverty 
alleviation depends on offering credit to the small -  scale industries. Will the 
WTO consider micro -credit and micro -enterprise at all? In my view, there 
must be a chapter, like TRIPS, in the Seattle Round on micro -enterprises 
supported by micro-credit. That chapter should be prepared by us and given to 
them for their reaction.    This would be 
218 

[ 27 APRIL, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
supported by all the South Asian countries, including China, which also has 
enormous problems in providing livelihood to its people. As I said, one in 
every third Asian is poor. We should prepare the first draft and give it to the 
rich countries for them to consider. In the preamble, you can quote their own 
words, from the G -7 and G -8 Resolutions on poverty, or the Copenhagen 
Summit, which has what is called an agreed text, or the World Food 
Conference, or the United Nations Poverty Reduction Goal of 2015, and then 
say that if you want to achieve all this, the trade policy should be geared to 
ensuring the survival not of the fittest, but of the weakest. This is the corr ect 
position. Even Dr. Swaminathan pleaded with him; he said "instead of just 
tinkering with the Resolution which the rich countries have prepared, why 
don't you prepare your own Resolution and have the elimination of poverty 
and also the other social concepts that you have in view, incorporated." All 
the richer countries in the world have committed themselves that they would 
support this kind of a resolution. So, you confront them with some kind of 
your own resolution. There will be support from all the de veloping countries 
in the world. In the recent summit conference which was held, we could see 
that there was a total revolt against the WTO. All the developing countries in 
the world had revolted and the Seattle Conference was a big fiasco. So, you 
can joi n those 135 countries. But our own Minister says that no question of 
any non-alignment is left. "We are free to take our own decision." Very good. 
You can take your own decision, but at the same time, I would say, unless you 
join with these people, I do not think India can have any kind of benefit out of 
this World Trade Organisation, which, in fact, is putting all kinds of barriers. 
You can see that they have their own interest. Inspite of the fact that they are 
signatories to the WTO, you will find that a ll kinds of protectionist measures 
have been adopted even by America. And now it is not only these fiscal 
measures, there are also some anti -tariff measures, other measures which they 
have adopted. They are saying "this has been produced by children, we wo n't 
accept it. Since there is an element of some kind of forced labour, we won't 
allow this kind of a thing." So, all these measures are also being adopted by 
them. And they are pleading to almost the entire Europe and North America, 
they are saying "we wo uld like to have the subsidy." A huge amount of 
subsidy is being paid in America for agriculture. 
But they are pleading with you.   And, without questioning them, 
219 

RAJYA SABHA  [ 27 APRIL, 2000] 
you were prepared to surrender yourselves to their dictat s. We did not want to 
find out whether it was in our interest or not. Now, I will come to the point 
which I have been, persistently, raising since the time Shri Barnala was the 
Minister of Agriculture and who was also in charge of Public Distribution. 
The question was about the import of sugar. Knowing full well that India had 
enough stocks at its disposal for the requirements of the country, -  not only 
that, we also had the bufferstock which are maintained by the co -operative 
sugar factories; they were available with us — in spite of the fact that sugar 
was being allowed to be imported, when I raised this issue, they said, "No, no, 
it has been going on since 1992." I do not know if this was correct; you have 
to go deep into the matter and find out what the position was in 1992. And, 
what was the position in 1996, when you did it? Sugar was on the OGL. They 
were subsidising right from 300 dollars per tonne to almost 3,000 dollars per 
tonne, and it was a clear case of dumping sugar in India. And, when I raised  
the question: "Why don't you increase your excise duty so that we have a 
level-playing field, and can you compete with those people who are 
subsidised to such a huge extent?" Barnalaji said, "I agree with you", and 
when he went to the Cabinet, it was turn ed down. You owe a certain 
explanation, Mr. Minister, as to what exactly was the reason that when the 
local cultivators were suffering, you wanted to create a condition by which the 
local sugar cultivators were totally destroyed. You don't want any policy to be 
followed which, ultimately, is going to benefit these cultivators! It is against 
the cultivators that you did the entire thing? And, unfortunately, for us, sugar 
was imported from Pakistan, from the Prime Minister of the 
country...(Interruptions) It was the then Prime Minister, of course. It is 
military rule now. It was the Prime Minister of Pakistan who was interested in 
exporting sugar to India, and the entire transaction was in foreign currency. 
This foreign currency has been utilised against India  by the ISI, and, if I were 
to make this kind of an allegation -  though I don't want to make it - that this 
was an anti -national act that you have done; you should, at least, explain to 
me as to why it is that the proposal of the Agriculture Ministry was turned 
down in the Cabinet. We were not expecting it. It was 10 -12 per cent and we 
wanted it to be increased to 60 per cent. Even 60 per cent would not bring us 
on a level -playing field at all If it was being subsidised in such a huge way, 
how can it be on a level -playing field? So, in order to bring them on par, you 
had to increase the excise duty. 
220 

[ 27 APRIL, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Knowing what has happened, I am, therefore, requesting you to kindly let me 
know what exactly was the reason. At least, let me  understand whether this 
was a reasonable view that you had. We will be satisfied if you give us a 
proper explanation. Otherwise, this will go against you, Mr. Minister. 
Now, regarding PDS, -  it is being said that this has been bifurcated 
and it is the other Minister who is dealing with the matter -  a rumour is going 
on that the whole thing is going to be repeated, and that, this time, sugar is 
going to be completely free. This was done when Shri Morarji Desai was 
there, and it was done for a temporary adva ntage, for reasons best known to 
them; but I do not know what those reasons were, though, everybody 
understands it. For a momentary gain, you discontinue the well laid -out 
policy and you say that you are going to free sugar. 
There must be someone who is go ing to be the beneficiary and that 
is why I request you not to indulge in this kind of strategy, which ultimately, 
is going to create almost a question of credibility of the Government. The 
Government will lose all its credibility and again have a momentar y gain, as 
the multinationals are doing. They will come here, sustain the losses, but kill 
their competitors and, five years later, they will demand more than double the 
price. Exactly the same thing is going to be repeated. If the cultivator is no 
more interested in sugarcane, a stage is going to come when again you will 
have to impose an entire system which, in fact, was in vogue, but it will be at 
the tremendous cost of the nation. For God's sake, don't try to impose such 
Governments which ultimately are going to be very dangerous for the 
stability of the country. There is only one point. So far as agricultural 
production is concerned, as you have to go to the rescue of the small and 
marginal farmers, I will request you that you have to provide the cultiv ators 
with good amount of irrigation. Where the dry land farmer is there, watershed 
management- should be properly done. Where surface irrigation is possible, 
try to provide him with that kind of irrigation facility. Next is electricity. I am 
realty sorry to say that both in irrigation potential as well as in electricity 
generation, we have failed, and failed very miserably. In the two successive 
plans, I find, on both the counts, the Government has failed, and everytime , 
some explanation or the other has been given, but that explanation is not 
going to suffice. It is not going to add to your agricultural production. If you 
want to double your agricultural pioduction, if you give them irrigation 
facilities, I am sure that you will have three crops in a year  and with that, you 
will be able to add to 
221 

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 APRIL, 2000] 
5.00 PM 
your foodgrain production. Now, with electricity, the kind of situation in 
which we are, we find, that, everyday almost there is a complete breakdown 
of electricity for h ours together. Even in Delhi you don't get electricity. What 
about the villages? There, they have a separate system and they just take out. 
So, he has to keep quiet. He has no alternative. He cannot demonstrate. He 
cannot create conditions for the Government where it would be impossible for 
you to function.. So, he has to quietly suffer the whole thing and, ultimately, it 
is a fall in agricultural production which is going to be the fall -out of the 
entire process. So, how are we going to continue with this kind of situation? 
Yesterday only, there was a question about PLF and Maharashtra's example 
was quoted by Shri Kumaramangalam, saying that you have surplus of power, 
but you are short of power during the peak hours. It is true. During peak 
hours, unless the capacity is given, I don't think there is any alternative. But 
what is the peaking capacity that you are trying to give? It is gas -based power 
plant and gas -based power plants are the worst and a very costly kind of 
electricity that you can think of. You  are giving counter -guarantee knowing 
full well that all the State Electricity Boards are in the red. Not even one is in 
a sound economic position. If counter -guarantee is given by the Government 
then, of course, you will have to shell out - from the Govern ment of India's 
Central funds. I hope everybody understands, but when we ask them on what 
basis you are trying to give counter -guarantee we just get evasive replies, 
giving some excuses or the other. Take, for example, the agreement which 
was entered into with Enron. 
Right from the Maharasthra State Government to the Central 
Government, I have been pursuing this matter to find out what kind of 
agreement has been entered into. Cheaper electricity cannot be taken by the 
Electricity Board. It is the Enron electricity, though that is very costly. Unless, 
the whole thing is exhausted by them, you can't get cheaper electricity. That is 
how the agreement is, I am told. I do not have any authentic reports as such. 
But if that is the position, then, of course, we are  in a very terrible situation. I 
don't think that with this kind of infrastructure being available, you can think 
of having any kind of food production programme that the Government is 
contemplating. Having gone into all the aspects of the question, at lea st, I am 
now forced to come to  this conclusion that you only talk of the good of the 
kisan, you only talk very 
222 

[ 27 APRIL, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
loud about them, but when it comes to deciding the policies, you are actually 
anti-kisan, you are anti -poor. That is why I tell you, unless you devise pro -
kisan policies, some of your allies even will almost force you and they will 
faithfully report to the Prime Minister the feeling of most of the allies of the 
Government. Then only they will sit down quietly. ...(Interruptions)... I am 
not making any allegation against you. This is the conclusion I draw after 
going through the entire thing. I have these two reports. I have quoted from 
the Standing Committee's reports. I have quoted from this interview of Mr. 
Swaminathan. So, the assumption is that your policies are anti- poor, your 
policies are anti -kisan and unless you restore this subsidy again, I don't think 
you can claim to be in favour of kisans and being their champion.. With these 
words, I thank you for giving me this opportunity. 
SHRI M. VENKAIAH NAIDU (Karnataka) : Sir, he may have been 
keenly observing. But being such a senior Member, he has forgotten that the 
subsidy of the order of Rs. 1000/ - per tonne for urea was withdrawn in 1991. 
If that is pro -kisan, how can this be anti -kisan? You should realty enlighten 
the House. 
SHRI S. B. CHAVAN: Mr. Naidu, how long will go on giving one 
excuse or the other? 
SHRI M.VENKAH NAIDU: Only for one year. After five years, I 
cannot give it.

SHRI YADLAPATI VENKAT RAO (Andhra Pradesh) : Mr. Vice -
Chairman, Sir, thank you for giving me an opportunity. 
I rise to support the Budget on Agriculture Demands. 
India is predominantly an agriculture country, with 73% of its 
population consisting of farmers, agricult ure labourers, artisans, etc., who 
live on agriculture. Bapuji, rightly said, "India lives in its villages", and he 
was proud in saying that he is a kisan from Gujarat. But, Sir, even after 52 
years of independence, the provisions of basic services in rural areas, the 
heart of the nation, are far from satisfactory. Sir, 40% villages are without 
proper roads, 1.8 lakh villages do not have primary schools within one 
kilometre, and 4.5 lakh villages have drinking water problems. This is the 
rural scenario. And  even after 52 years of independence, we are not able to 
provide the basic minimum services. 
If we take India's agriculture, two -third is rain -fed and only one -
third is irrigated. So, there is every necessity to improve the rain -fed 
agriculture, as my other friends have also pointed out, to increase the 
229 

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 APRIL, 2000] 
production that would be sufficient to feed the teeming millions of the Indian 
population. If we talk about the production of foodgrains, it was 50 million 
tonnes when we b ecome independent, and now the production stands at 200 
million tonnes. This could be achieved because the farmers are innovative and 
they are ready to implement the new agro -economic practices given by the 
scientists. But what reward the farmer is getting  for this, except that he is 
being praised as Annadata. He has got his children to be educated, to be 
married, and he has also to take care of the health of the family. During the 
Green Revolution, a slogan was given, requesting farmers to "produce more 
or perish." Now, the farmers are not given full credit to their efforts. They are 
producing more and perishing also because of lack of remunerative prices. 
The farmers are responsible for the increase in food production and 
transforming the country from 'the  begging bowl to a bread basket.' 
Simultaneously, the country should realise the various constraints in 
production. Sir, various things have to be looked into, namery, supplying 
sufficient quantity of high -yielding variety of seeds, high cost of fertiliser s, 
scarcity of water, meeting the timely and sufficient credit needs of the 
farmers, etc. The credit requirement is to the tune of Rs. 44,635 crores, but 
only a credit of Rs. 41,800 crores is arranged. Sir, 90% of the farming 
community is indebted and their credit requirements are not met. They have to 
borrow at huge rates of interest from the private money -lenders. In 
agriculture, credit is an important input. If it is not met in time, the farmer will 
suffer. As Pandit Nehruji rightly said, "anything can wait, but not agriculture". 
Hence, the credit requirement of the farmers should be met amply. 
Regarding the Commission on Agricultural Costs and Prices, many 
of its members do not have any practical knowledge of agriculture. Those 
who have not seen the vill ages and do not know that a bund exists in the 
fields, are deciding the fate of the farming community. Sir, the real farmers 
should be there in the CACP. The CACP should announce the prices well in 
advance of the season, which has not been done so far. Cer tain realities which 
are involved in the process of agriculture should be taken into consideration 
while fixing the prices of agriculture commodities. 
There is every need for a crop insurance scheme throughout the 
country, for all the crops. The farmer dep ends on the vagaries of nature, and if 
there is no insurance protection for the crop he is raising, he will loose 
everything.   The farmer toils day-and- night, and his entire family is 
230 

[ 27 APRIL, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
engaged in producing foodgrains to feed the nation, perishing himself. If crop 
insurance is there, to a large extent, he will be safe. Crop insurance should 
cover all the crops, and the village should be taken as a unit, instead of 
mandals, while assessing the loss during times of damage. T he premium that 
has to be paid by the small and marginal farmers on account of this should 
also be minimum. 
It is a long -pending cry of the farming community that a National 
Agriculture Policy should be announced. The industrialists who form a small 
section of the population, are having an Industrial Policy since long back. But 
the farming community which constitutes the bulk of the population, has been 
deprived of this till today. The government should take immediate initiative 
to formulate a National Agri cultural Policy so that the farmers will have 
protection from all the vagaries of nature and that they will have a 
remunerative price etc. 
Our Chief Minister, Shri Chandra Babu Naidu, is giving a great 
thrust to agriculture in Andhra Pradesh by inducing the farmers to produce 
more by adopting new technologies and at a less cost. Many Kisan Melas are 
being held by the Agriculture Marketing Committees to bring awareness to 
the farming community. The Government has formed the Water -users 
Associations, and for the first time in the annals of the history of Andhra 
Pradesh, rights have been given to fanners to get water to their fields. Rs.142 
crores was allotted and spent. The channels were repaired in a very big way 
Because of this, water is reaching the tail -ends in time, as a  result of which, 
there is a bumper crop of paddy this year. 
When the price of chillies fell down last year, the Chief Minister 
took immediate steps for market intervention operations. Chillies from the 
fanners were purchased, and they wer e rescued to a great extent. Another 
important programme for the benefit of the farmers is the Water -shed 
Programme, and it has been taken up in a big way in Andhra Pradesh. Lakhs 
of acres of land is being brought under cultivation, and increased production 
has been made possible. Shri Anna Hazare, the social reformer from 
Maharashtra, visited Andhra Pradesh, saw the functioning of water -sheds and 
complemented our Chief Minister, Shri Chandra Babu Naidu, for making the 
running water work in a way that the precious top soil is not eroded. 
231 

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 APRIL, 2000] 
Regarding tobacco, this year the production is 160 million kgs. 
Though the crop size is of 100 million tonnes, the production is to the tune of 
160 million kgs. The tobacco farmers are in d istress. At the instance of our 
Chief Minister and MPs, the Union Commerce Minister was pleased to make 
arrangements With the State Trading Corporation to buy tobacco at the last 
year's price plus 10 per cent. I am happy that the Central Government came to  
the rescue of the tobacco farmers. 
The cotton farmer is also in a miserable position. The crop has been 
lost in drought, and what little crop he has got is not fetching a good price. I 
request the Government to direct the Cotton Corporation of India to en ter the 
market, stay in the market and make purchases in a big way to help the farmer 
from being exploited by middlemen and traders. 
I am coming to a close, Sir. 
A word about fertilizers. The consumption of fertilizers in the year 
1961 was 0.21 million metric tonnes, whereas in 1999-2000, it was to the tune 
of 19.1 million metric tonnes. In countries like Japan, China etc. where the 
fertilizer consumption is more, the production is more. The recent hike in the 
prices of fertilizers will put a heavy burden o n the farmers. I earnestly request 
the Government to roll back the prices of fertilizers.  Otherwise, the 
production will go down. 
Before I conclude, I am reminded of Goldsmith's poem, The 
Deserted Village, wherein he wrote: 
"Bold peasantry, the country's pride, When once 
destroyed can never be supplied." 
Thank you.

SHRI A VIJAYA RAGHAVAN (Kerala): Hon. Vice -Chairman, Sir, 
we have heard the speeches of the Members, supporting the Demands for 
Grants of the Ministry of Agriculture and congratulating the Government for 
the present policy being pursued by the NDA 
Sir, here, we are giving a rosy picture that the country is advancing, 
that there is sufficient, food, that all things are good and that

agriculture is improving. On the one side, we are saying all these things: on 
the other hand, in reality, suicides are being reported from the villages of 
India and migration is going on from villages to towns, not in thousands but 
in millions and millions. 
People are moving from one area to another area. From Bihar, they 
are moving to Pubjab and so on. Migration is not from a village to a town. 
While we talk so much of developments in the field of agriculture, we lose 
sight of the unemployment, particularly, in the rural part of the country. Even 
now agriculture employs 80 per cent of our population. As a result of 
migration, it is the women who have to suffer the most because, after the 
migration of their male counter -parts, it is  they who have to take care of the 
entire family. While the hon. Minister talks of growth in agriculture, he 
forgets to take note of the pauperisation of the peasents. Our achievements in 
agriculture are for the benefit of the rich peasantry. While pursuin g our 
policies for the development of agriculture, the Government should also look 
to the interests of the poor and marginal farmers. They form 70 per cent of 
the rural population. I regret to say that successive Governments in the 
country have neglected t heir interests. The present BJP Government has 
totally failed to safeguard their interests. 
My learned friends like Chavanji and Janeshwar Mishraji have 
already explained how investment in agriculture has been coming down. If 
you go through the record sinc e the globalisation process started, you will

crores. But, if you look at it in real terms, the am ount of allotment was less 
than the earlier Plan. Non -utilisation of the funds further brought down the 
share of investment in agriculture, further, if you look at the demand for 
investment during last year, you will find that it was Rs. 18,253 crores. But

experience, as Chavanji has explained, you will find that the Agriculture

down. 
Now , I come to the problems faced by the common people. If you 
go into the details, you will find that the foodgrains production has been

country, there are crops like plantain and paddy. Crop insurance scheme 
should be extended to this type of crops also. It should also be extended to 
horticultural crops like mango and coconut. Nowadays, in Tamil Nadu, 
insects attack the entire coconut. ...and the result is that the coconut 
production is declining. In this way, for all agricultural crops, there should be 
crop insurance. The crop insurance should be made compulsory for all the 
small farmers because for non-loanees it is not compulsory.  The premium for 
the small and the medium farmers should be nominal so that they are given 
due protection. I would also like to submit that soil testing is very necessary. 
It has been reported that in the entire country only 1800 mo bile soil testing 
laboratories are functioning. My humble request is that these mobile soil -
testing laboratories should be installed in each panchyat unit. The 
agriculturists should not be made to go to a particular place for getting their 
soil tested. Ins tead of that the Government can arrange mobile soil testing 
laboratories because after every harvest the soil is not preserved property. 
There was an article two or three days back suggesting that nearly 50 per cent 
of the produce is getting wasted because  no proper cold storage facility is 
available to the farmers. For this purpose also, the farmers should be given 
facilities for starting cold storages. In this way, they can store their produce 
and can sell it at a profitable rate. Sir, proper attention sh ould be paid to the 
needs of the agriculturists, agriculture should be made knowledge intensive, 
and appreciation of agriculture would help to attract and retain youth in 
farming.   Agriculture should also be made our 
269 

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 APRIL, 2000] 
primary sector activity and it should be made an intellectually stimulating and 
economically rewarding employment. This should be extended to all the 
villages so that agriculture becomes attractive so that educated persons also 
resort to it. 
SHRI N.R. DASARI (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Vice- Chairman, Sir, I 
rise to protest against the indifference to our agricultural sector. I will try to 
explain how this indifference has been displayed in this Budget. Even after 50 
years of Independence and planning, the agricultur al production in our 
country has not yet stabilised. The country's agriculture is still dependent on 
the vagaries of the monsoon. In fact, the agricultural sector is facing a 
multidimensional crisis today. The most alarming feature in this year has been 
a decline in public investment in agriculture. I would repeat that there has 
been a decline in public investment in agriculture. I would have been happy if 
Chavanji had been present here because he tried to throw the entire blame on 
the present regime. But, it is not like this. Till the 5th Plan, the outlay for 
agriculture and allied activities had been 12.5 per cent. In some annual plans it 
was around 16 per cent. But, from 6th Plan onwards, outlays for agriculture 
and allied sectors started showing a decreasing trend from 6.1 per cent in the 
6th Plan to 5.8 per cent in the 7th Plan.   It became 5.2 per cent in the 8th 
Plan. 
During 1997-98, it was just 3.1 per cent and during 1998- 99, it was 
slightly better at 4.4 per cent. But, for 1999- 2000, though the Budget 
Estimates for agriculture and allied activities was Rs. 3,736 crores, the 
Revised Estimates was only Rs. 3,017 crores That is, it was only 3.15 per cent 
of the total Outlay. The Budget Estimates for the current financial year ie., for 
2000-2001, is only  Rs. 3,623 crores, which makes 3.1 per cent of the total 
Outlay of Rs. 1,17,334 crores. The Department of Animal Husbandry and 
Dairying, which should have been given more importance, seems to have been 
neglected. Though the Budget Estimates for this Depart ment, which is in the 
agricultural sector, was Rs. 382 crores for 1999 -2000, the Revised Estimates 
was only Rs. 225' crores and the estimated outlay in the current Budget is only 
Rs. 300 crores. So, Sir, there is nothing in the Budget which shows concern 
for attaining stability and steady growth in the agricultural sector. 
The changes at the domestic and international levels that have been 
brought in the nineties through economic reforms and globalisation have a 
270 

[ 27 APRIL, 2000]  RAJYA SABHA 
far-reaching impact on our agricultural sector. With the reduction in States' 
intervention, vulnerable sectors like agriculture have been affected in several 
ways - through cuts in public investments, slow -down in irrigation 
development, withdrawal of input subsidi es and deterioration in food security 
among other things ...(time -bell)... Sir, I have been waiting very patiently. I 
am a farmer myself and you should be kind enough to the actual farmers. 
Sir, during the period 1990 -91 to 1998- 99, when the economic 
reforms were implemented, the growth rates of total agricultural production 
as well as foodgrain production declined sharply. The overall growth rate of 
foodgrain production decelerated to 1.8 per cent per annum during the decade 
of nineties when compared to 3.54 per cent during eighties. 
Decline in productivity of our 12 major crops raises questions about 
the competitiveness of our agricultural products in the world markets.' The 
lifting of the Quantitative Restrictions on imports of 714 items from 1st April, 
2000, and the remaining 715 items by 1st April, 2001, will have the worst 
impact on India's agricultural production and crop patters, through low -priced 
imports entering the country.

SHRI N. R. DASARI: The new economic policies aim at promoting 
agricultural exports. This will lead to the entry of MNCs and the Indian 
corporate sector into t he agricultural sector resulting in changing the pattern 
of land holdings through dispossession of small and marginal farmers from 
their land. The pressure for complete removal of the ceiling limit on land 
holdings is an indication of the future trend. Thi s is a dangerous trend. Land 
reforms should be implemented vigorously and effectively in all the States 
and the Government should see to it that land reforms process is not reversed. 
The Finance Minister had emphasized the need to set up a national 
commission on land use policy. I welcome it. But, while constituting this 
commission, care should be taken to see that not only experts but eminent 
representatives of agriculture and agricultural labourers also are included. 
While evolving a comprehensive land use policy, the Government should

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 APRIL, 2000] 
also see that land is not concentrated in the hands of the corporate sector, 
whether indigenous or foreign, who may come forward to develop such waste 
lands, dry lands, etc. Sir, I am comin g to an end. These are some of the 
problems being faced by our agricultural sector which have to be tackled on a 
priority basis to make Indian agriculture more productive and more 
competitive in the next few years to come. A new national policy on 
agriculture has to be evolved giving more emphasis on increasing foodgrain 
production and productivity.

developed on the lines of join t forest management cooperatives. Water -
management and watershed management technologies should be given top 
priority to maintain required availability of the present resource.

agriculture, animal husbandry, fisheries, forestry and allied vocations which 
should be  duly  recognised while evolving  a new  Agricultural Policy.

SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMAD KHAN (DURRU) (Rajasthan) : Mr. 
Vice-Chairman, Sir, lately, two of the burning issues which have been under . 
scrutiny in the country are  subsidies on fertilisers and drought. Therefore, a 
long-term planning for water -harvesting and water -management is required. 
Both these issues are connected with agriculture and, therefore, have an impact 
on the vast majority of India's population. The Government is still to come out 
with a comprehensive National Agriculture Policy to address these issues. 
Let us not forget that we are primarily a rural nation and most of our 
people depend on agriculture for their livelihood. Therefore, development of 
agriculture, particularly, in the rain -fed and drought -prone areas where 
poverty is extreme, should be accorded high priority. 
This would call for substantial capital formation in agriculture and 
investment in the areas where productivity has been relatively l ow. As the 
agriculture sector still employs about two-thirds of our total workforce, 
272 

[ 27 APRIL, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
greater investment in agriculture, including agro -industries, need to be 
mobilized to enhance employment opportunities and create greater prosperity 
in rural areas. 
Agriculture is not a fashionable subject; it is not high -profile or 
newsworthy. But agriculture creates national wealth -  it is our greatest and 
most renewable national resource. 
In our mindless haste to ape the West, by copyin g the western model 
of development, we have committed the error of turning our backs on ancient 
wisdom and proven practices that have sustained our people for countless 
centuries. Our fanners have been misled into abandoning the old organic 
methods of cult ivation which nurtured the soil and nourished the people -  
what was once known as Rishi Kheti. 
We need to ask ourselves if we have paid enough attention to 
dangers of chemical farming, which has poisoned our fertile soil and polluted 
our great rivers and c reated deadly health hazards, many of which are as yet 
unknown. The quantity of chemical fertilisers used is mounting year by year, 
and with it, the quantum of subsidies goes up. What many city- dwellers do 
not realise, and what the present Government is no t keen to acknowledge, is 
that every farmer has to apply increased doses of chemical fertiliser to his 
land every year -  to counter the degrading quality of his land caused by the 
use of chemicals. And each year, his land is further impoverished. The only 
sector that gains is the chemical and fertiliser industry. 
This has been borne out by various studies. I would like to refer to 
the findings of Dr. Y.M Upadhya of the Wheat Research Station, Indore that 
the input-output ratio for wheat has fallen from 1:16  in the early eighties to 
just about 1:7 at present. 
What is more  chemical fertilisers, together with hybrid seeds, 
weaken plant health and increase the susceptibility of plants to disease. This 
leads to ever-increasing doses of pesticides, many of which are infused in the 
fruit, vegetables and grain which we consume. 
I have worked for many years in agricultural areas and I have seen 
farmers over-burdened with the high costs of chemical agriculture. I have also 
seen some innovative people from the corporate world taking up farming with 
a view to trying to solve, in their own small way, some of these serious 
problems. 
 
 
273 
 

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 APRIL, 2000] 
In my own constituency, in District Alwar of Rajasthan, there is a 
farmer who is experimenting with bio- dynamics on his 40 -acre farm, on 
which he grows fruits, vegetables and ground crops. He is experimenting with 
organic farming and bio -dynamic farming, based on the ancient wisdom of 
our Vedas and Shastras. 
We need to revive Javik Kheti or Rishi Kheti on a much larger scale. 
The eminent German scientist and philosopher, Rudolph Steiner, had, as far 
back as 1924, drawn on ancient Indian sources to re -propound the principles 
of bio- dynamic farming which is being practised by enlightened fanners in 
many western countries. This system leads to output levels similar to those of 
conventional chemical farming and has the added advantage of not only 
reducing soil degradation but also actually enriching the soil on an on- going 
basis. Organic farming uses only cow -dung to fertilise the fields. This 
eliminates the problems of toxins poisoning the soil and water. (Time belt)     
One minute. 
The food produced is, therefore, healthy and free from toxins. This 
also reduces the costs to the farmer and thereby cuts down on the need for 
fertilizer subsidy. Under chemical farming, one acre of land under wheat 
requires Rs. 1,280/ - worth of chemical fertilizers, whereas under the organic 
methods, the costs are negligible. Various studies have shown that the water 
requirement where chemical farming is done, is 25 per cent more than where 
organic farming is done. 
Sir, I appeal, through you, to this august House and the Government: 
Let us join hands and redefine our agricultural policies by reviving 
and popularising organic methods of cultivation. Let us elevate agriculture to 
the predominant status it deserves and improving the health of our ailing 
Mother Earth. 
Thank you, Sir.
